# `==` between two structs, colors included, compares them field by field on
# every target, and a test reads a package const as the page does.
#
# JavaScript's === is an object's identity, and html wrote it for any struct
# but a payload enum's payload, so two colors written alike were unequal. And
# an html test runs in a module beside the page, which finds the page's names
# on window: its funcs were published there and its consts were not, so a
# test reading a const map -- or calling a func the optimizer inlined into a
# read of one -- threw `pairs is not defined`, which the run reported with no
# message at all.

sngl test --platform=none app.sngl
stdout 'ok +1 tests, 0 failures'
sngl test --platform=html app.sngl
stdout 'ok +1 tests, 0 failures'
sngl test --platform=bubbletea --language=go app.sngl
stdout 'ok +1 tests, 0 failures'
sngl test --platform=fyne --language=go app.sngl
stdout 'ok +1 tests, 0 failures'
sngl test --platform=gtk4 --language=go app.sngl
stdout 'ok +1 tests, 0 failures'
sngl test --platform=android --language=kotlin app.sngl
stdout 'ok +1 tests, 0 failures'

-- app.sngl --
import test "sngl:test"
import ui "sngl:ui"

struct Pair {
    left  int
    right int
}

const pairs map[string, Pair] = {"a" = Pair{left=1, right=2}}

const tints map[string, color] = {"a" = #a8a77a}

component page ui.node {
    var p = Pair{left=1, right=2}
    ui.text(value="{p.left}")
}

func testStructsCompareByValue(t test.Test, c page) {
    t.assert(c.p == Pair{left=1, right=2})
    t.assert(pairs["a"] == Pair{left=1, right=2})
    t.assert(tints.get("a", #000000) == #a8a77a)
    t.assert(tints.get("a", #000000) != #a8a77b)
}

ui.window {
    page()
}
